title: The One With The Blind Dates

jokes.text: You remembered to put clothes on this morning.
jokes.setup: Ross greets Rachel with 'Morning, roomie' as she arrives, implying normalcy of cohabitation.
jokes.punchline: Ross noting she remembered to put clothes on implies she previously hadn't — immediately establishing a funny domestic chaos dynamic.
jokes.explanation: Light, competent opener that establishes the living situation comedy. The implication of Rachel having been seen without clothes before is a quick, functional laugh but not particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Hey, good morning! Did you sleep well?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, great! Why do you ask?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, you're not wearing any pants.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

jokes.text: Fifth day's the charm.
jokes.setup: Ross says she remembered to put clothes on this morning.
jokes.punchline: Rachel confirms it took five days — a riff on 'third time's the charm' — casually admitting she's been walking around without clothes for four days.
jokes.explanation: Sharp wordplay on the idiom 'third time's the charm' that also confirms the previous joke's implication. The economy is excellent — four words do a lot of work. Good construction but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, you know what they say — third time's a charm!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Although, technically, this is the fifth time I'm wearing this outfit.

jokes.text: And when does she stop crying all night?
jokes.setup: Ross warmly tells Rachel to stay as long as she wants, projecting gracious host energy.
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to asking when the baby stops crying — the warmth was performative, he's exhausted.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom bait-and-switch: the gracious line undercut by the selfish concern. Functional and well-timed but not particularly original — the sleep-deprived parent/host joke is well-worn territory.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Of course you should stay! We want you here.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Although, you'll have to start paying rent, and my apartment's getting really crowded, and honestly the utilities bill is already insane...

jokes.text: Hey! You're not naked. Heh.
jokes.setup: Joey arrives and greets Rachel, echoing the earlier naked joke.
jokes.punchline: Joey's version of a compliment is relief that she's dressed — but his 'heh' implies it's also a mild disappointment, perfectly in character.
jokes.explanation: The callback works because Joey's version reveals his character: where Ross was relieved/annoyed, Joey is simultaneously polite and transparently a little disappointed. The 'heh' does a lot of character work. High character integration score justified.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wow, you're wearing clothes!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I got dressed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, but... you're wearing clothes.

jokes.text: She's probably exhausted from all that adorable screaming she did last night.
jokes.setup: Joey is told Emma fell back to sleep.
jokes.punchline: Joey calls the screaming 'adorable' — the word is sincere affection but the content (screaming all night) undercuts it perfectly, expressing the exasperation everyone's feeling while maintaining the social politeness.
jokes.explanation: Competent joke about the duality of loving a baby while being tortured by one. The word choice of 'adorable screaming' is the engine — it's a small but effective juxtaposition.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's sleeping because I gave him a little warm milk and rocked him gently.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, how adorable. A baby who needs constant attention and makes noise at 3 AM.

jokes.text: ...when you walk in on a woman using a breast pump — Yeah, that'll do it.
jokes.setup: Ross is reassuring Joey that his feelings for Rachel are gone.
jokes.punchline: The breast pump revelation is hilariously specific and visceral — it's the most un-romantic image imaginable, used as evidence his attraction has been killed. Joey's 'yeah, that'll do it' as knowing validation is perfect.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's stronger jokes. The specificity of 'breast pump' as the libido-killer is bold and funny — it's not 'something unsexy,' it's the most specific, vulnerable, clinical possible image. Joey's deadpan confirmation adds a second beat that lands. The joke earns a high score for structure and economy — it's also genuinely character-specific to both men.

jokes.text: It's not like it's a divorce. — Well, actually it... — It's not a divorce. It is not a divorce!
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to be philosophical about his split with Rachel, saying 'it's not like it's a divorce.'
jokes.punchline: Joey begins to point out that it technically IS (they were married), and Ross preemptively shuts him down with increasing desperation — the joke is that Ross knows it's a divorce but can't bear to hear it said.
jokes.explanation: Excellent use of Ross's history (multiple divorces) as comedic architecture. The joke works on two levels: the audience knows Ross's divorce record, and the panic in 'It is not a divorce!' reveals Ross's self-deception in real time. Character integration is very high — this joke only works because it's Ross, and his desperation is perfectly consistent with his established neurosis about being 'the divorce guy.'

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A breakup isn't like a divorce.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, it's—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know what you're going to say. You're right, I'm sorry. You're always right. I'm an idiot. A complete idiot who knows nothing about relationships or anything else.

jokes.text: Ooh, strained plums. We haven't tried that yet. — Goody!
jokes.setup: Monica lists Emma's available baby food options.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's sarcastic 'Goody!' — the flat delivery shows just how dismal his domestic life has become that this passes for exciting food news.
jokes.explanation: Functional sarcasm joke that hints at Chandler's boredom/desperation. Works as a quick character beat but isn't memorable on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Come on, give me some names. You must know some girls.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, oh! Yeah, yeah, there's... there's...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? I got nothing. I got nothing.

jokes.text: You know what's crazy? These jars. What is there, like, two bites in here?
jokes.setup: Joey and Monica are having a sincere conversation about Ross and Rachel's relationship.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, bored, interrupts with a completely mundane complaint about baby food jar sizes — a total non-sequitur that reveals how out of the emotional loop he is.
jokes.explanation: Good use of Chandler as the grounded, bored observer amid earnest relationship talk. The randomness of the complaint works because it's so mundane it circles back to funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Try this strained plums baby food.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh wow, strained plums! Yeah, that's exactly what I've always wanted. Finally, someone's made a food that tastes like it's already been digested.

jokes.text: Yes. And they should name one of their kids Joey. I may not have kids. Someone's gotta carry on the family name.
jokes.setup: Monica says Ross and Rachel should have more children.
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately redirects the conversation to making sure his name lives on — the logic is both completely self-centered and strangely poignant. 'I may not have kids' adds an unexpectedly melancholy dimension.
jokes.explanation: A good Joey joke that works because it's both funny and weirdly sincere — Joey genuinely seems to believe this is a reasonable request. His logic is impeccable within his own worldview. Plants a seed for the later callback about naming the baby Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So Ross and Rachel are finally getting their act together?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, how much baby food is in one of these jars? This is like a thimble full of carrots. What is this, for ants?

jokes.text: I had this date last night. Yuck! But we should probably keep it down, she's still in the bedroom.
jokes.setup: Monica says she had a date last night and it was 'yuck,' implying the date went badly.
jokes.punchline: She then says they should keep it down because 'she's still in the bedroom' — the date is a woman still at her place, completely recontextualizing 'yuck' as complicated rather than just bad.
jokes.explanation: Nice misdirection — we assume the bad date left; the reveal that the woman is still there opens several possibilities (Did they hook up? Is it really bad? Is she a Phoebe client?). The ambiguity is funnier than any specific answer. Good construction.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Come on! You gotta name the kid Joey. Think about it — a little Joey running around the city, living out all my dreams. Plus, the kid gets my good looks, my charm, my acting talent — it's a win-win!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, those are your dreams. The kid might want to be an accountant or something.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: An accountant? Dude, why would you curse our child like that?

jokes.text: You know what the best part of it is? I get to do my plan laugh: [LAUGHS MANIACALLY]
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Joey hatch a plan to set Ross and Rachel up with terrible dates.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe explicitly announces that the best part of having a plan is getting to do her 'plan laugh' — then executes a full maniacal villain laugh, treating it as a formal part of the scheme.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The meta quality of announcing the joke type before performing it, combined with Phoebe's complete sincerity, is genuinely funny. It's a Phoebe-specific piece of comedy — she has codified a 'plan laugh' as part of her scheming ritual. High character integration justified. The joke also sets up multiple callbacks throughout the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This date was a disaster. She talked the entire time, complained about everything, and then ordered the most expensive thing on the menu.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what'd you do?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I did what any gentleman would do. I sat there and suffered through it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Please tell me you at least said goodbye.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm about to.

dialogue.speaker: Bad Date
dialogue.line: Joey? Are you coming back to the table?

jokes.text: Joey joins the maniacal plan laugh, then Phoebe shushes him — 'Not so loud. We don't wanna wake up, uh...'
jokes.setup: Phoebe does her plan laugh; Joey enthusiastically joins.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe shushes him and trails off — implying she's already forgotten the name of the person sleeping nearby, and the elaborate plan is already slightly out of control.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke. Joey being shushed while doing the laugh he was just encouraged to do is a nice irony, and Phoebe forgetting the woman's name hints at the chaos beneath the 'plan.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Most excited about doing evil laugh

jokes.text: See, now, why would you assume that? Just because we're married? I will have you know that we are very hip, happening people. Now if you'll excuse me, I have to get back to reading the obituaries.
jokes.setup: Rachel asks Chandler and Monica if they're doing anything that night, implying they have no life.
jokes.punchline: Chandler launches a defensive protest about being 'hip and happening' — immediately undercut by revealing he was reading the obituaries, which is the least hip activity possible.
jokes.explanation: Classic setup/undercut structure executed well. The protest of 'we're hip and happening' followed immediately by the obituaries reveal is a textbook ironic self-own, but the specificity of 'obituaries' (not just the crossword or TV Guide) makes it funnier. Chandler's voice in the dialogue is very consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Mwahahaha!

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: What are you laughing about?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, nothing, nothing...

jokes.text: You want a job? Turn off Oprah and send out a résumé.
jokes.setup: Monica is talking enthusiastically about Rachel's 'womanhood' and 'needs,' getting somewhat preachy.
jokes.punchline: Chandler cuts through Monica's inspirational rambling with blunt, practical advice — the comedic whiplash from Monica's earnestness to Chandler's pragmatism.
jokes.explanation: Sharp one-liner from Chandler. The abruptness is the whole joke — he drops the supportive-friend pretense to give Rachel actual advice, and the specificity of 'Oprah' grounds it in mid-2000s reality. Economy is very high — the line does its work efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We are cool! We're on the cutting edge of society.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: In fact, I just bought tickets to see Cher.

jokes.text: Suddenly I wish I was reading my own name.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just delivered a terrifying list of Emma's needs: pooping around the clock, hair-grabbing, screaming if left alone.
jokes.punchline: Chandler wishes he was listed in the obituaries — i.e., he'd rather be dead than babysit. The dark turn is a perfect Chandler response to impending domestic chaos.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. It callbacks to the obituaries joke immediately preceding it, adds a dark layer (wishing for death over babysitting), and does it in nine words. The economy is exceptional — 'my own name' rather than 'dead' makes it cleverer and more quotable. This joke earns its high scores: it's character-perfect Chandler, structured as a callback payoff, and delivers a dark laugh without being mean-spirited.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so you need to be honest with him. Tell him how you really feel.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And then update your resume, because you're going to need a backup plan.

jokes.text: It's this guy I used to massage. By 'massage' I mean hold down so he wouldn't turn over and flash me.
jokes.setup: Joey asks Phoebe who she set Rachel up with.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe redefines 'massage' to mean restraining someone from exposing themselves — the job description from hell delivered with cheerful matter-of-factness.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Phoebe joke. The 'by X I mean Y' structure is clean, and the revelation is specific and disturbing in a funny way. Only Phoebe would (a) have this experience, (b) consider such a person a 'dear friend,' and (c) describe it this calmly. High character integration justified.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, so if Emma gets fussy, you can give her a bottle. And if she cries after eating, just pat her back gently. Oh, and she's been a little constipated lately, so don't be alarmed if her stool is hard and clay-like. Actually, it's more of a greenish-brown color today. And the texture is sort of like—

jokes.text: She's this really boring woman. She's a teacher. — A teacher? — She's into history and foreign movies. And she loves puzzles. Come on, who loves puzzles?
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to set Ross up with someone terrible.
jokes.punchline: Everything Joey thinks is boring is actually Ross's perfect woman — history, foreign films, puzzles. Joey has inadvertently found Ross's soulmate while trying to ruin his night.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke that works on a sitcom-structural level — the audience is ahead of Joey, which creates dramatic irony. 'Who loves puzzles?' as a rhetorical question is funny because the answer is so obviously 'Ross.' Strong character integration for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, Monica was reading obituaries? What was she doing, looking for baby care tips?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I was reading about people who died peacefully in their sleep.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's your idea of a parenting book?

jokes.text: She even reads for pleasure! — Ugh. [JOEY SCOFFS]
jokes.setup: Joey and Phoebe are realizing they accidentally set Ross up with his perfect woman.
jokes.punchline: The final detail — she 'reads for pleasure' — is treated as the most damning attribute of all, with both characters reacting with disgust. Joey's scoff is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke. 'Reads for pleasure' as the final, unforgivable character flaw (from Joey's perspective) is a funny character-specific judgment. The shared disgust of Joey and Phoebe at literacy is a quick, effective laugh.

jokes.text: I'm not allowed to know smart women? — Joey? — I met her at the library. I went in to pee.
jokes.setup: Phoebe questions how Joey knows a woman like that (smart, literary).
jokes.punchline: Joey defends his right to know smart women, then immediately reveals he only went to the library to use the bathroom — the defense collapses under its own weight.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Joey briefly sounds principled ('I'm not allowed to know smart women?'), creating a small moment of dignity before the reveal annihilates it. 'I went in to pee' is the perfect Joey-specific answer — no other character on this or any show would say this. Economy is excellent (three words to detonate the joke). Character integration is as high as it gets for a one-liner — this joke could not exist without Joey Tribbiani.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She's got this thing where she just talks and talks about nothing. Just rambles on and on about her day, her thoughts, her feelings...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait a minute... She's perfect for Ross!

jokes.text: Ah, yes, the plan. Ho-ho-ho. — It's not Santa's plan.
jokes.setup: Joey does a 'ho-ho-ho' as an approximation of a villain laugh.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe corrects him — that's Santa Claus, not a villain — a weirdly specific and pedantic distinction that is very Phoebe.
jokes.explanation: A smart addition to the plan-laugh running gag. The distinction between 'ho-ho-ho' (Santa) and the maniacal laugh (villain) is funny because Phoebe takes it seriously as a matter of protocol. The joke has brevity working for it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, how do you know her?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I was at the library.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You go to the library?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, to pick up women. They love the Dewey Decimal System.

jokes.text: No, it's: [LAUGHS MANIACALLY] — Yeah, you know, it's not that fun. — No, I think we killed it.
jokes.setup: Phoebe demonstrates the correct plan laugh again after correcting Joey.
jokes.punchline: Joey admits it's not fun anymore; Phoebe agrees they've 'killed' the joke by overdoing it — a meta acknowledgment that the bit has run its course.
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta move — the show acknowledges the bit has been overdone, which is itself funny. 'I think we killed it' is a rare moment of sitcom self-awareness that works without being too cute. The joke earns its score for originality in this self-referential approach.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Mwahahaha! The plan is finally coming together!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What plan?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know, THE plan!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I don't know what plan you're talking about.

jokes.text: Don't cry, it's just a bit. I'm your Uncle Chandler. Funny is all I have!
jokes.setup: Chandler tries to entertain baby Emma, who starts crying when he moves away.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's desperate plea that 'funny is all I have' reveals a surprisingly existential self-assessment — he's literally begging a baby to validate his core identity. The desperation is both funny and weirdly poignant.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most memorable lines. 'Funny is all I have' works on multiple levels: it's immediately funny, it's a vulnerable character admission, and it perfectly encapsulates Chandler's self-image as the group's comedian. High character integration — Chandler has always defined himself by being the funny one, so this is both joke and character revelation simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Mwahahaha! Mwahahaha!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm practicing my evil laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, it's not working.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know.

jokes.text: Just so you know, I'm gonna be ovulating from tomorrow until the 6th. So don't touch yourself for the next 48 hours.
jokes.setup: Domestic scene with Chandler and Monica babysitting Emma.
jokes.punchline: Monica's clinical ovulation announcement — delivered as a matter-of-fact household notice — is funny for its complete lack of romance, treating sex as a scheduled fertility appointment.
jokes.explanation: Solid Monica joke. The ovulation scheduling is a running element of their storyline, and the clinical framing ('so don't touch yourself') is funny for its transactional bluntness. Very Monica — hyper-organized and direct even about intimacy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any worse with children?

jokes.text: I don't do that. — I'll try to stop.
jokes.setup: Monica tells Chandler not to touch himself for 48 hours.
jokes.punchline: Chandler denies it, then immediately says 'I'll try to stop' — confirming it without admitting it. The contradiction in two consecutive lines is the whole joke.
jokes.explanation: Tight two-beat joke. The structure is clean — denial then immediate self-betrayal. Economy is excellent; the whole exchange is four words. Not particularly original but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You can't keep doing this, Chandler. You need to stop.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not doing anything!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I wasn't. But now you've got me thinking about it.

jokes.text: Today is the 6th. — No, it's not. Look. — Yes, it's also 2003.
jokes.setup: Monica says she's ovulating until the 6th; Chandler realizes today might be the 6th.
jokes.punchline: Monica shows the calendar to prove him wrong; Chandler confirms that yes, it IS the 6th — the calendar also shows the year (2003), which is useless information delivered as if it's a knockout argument.
jokes.explanation: Good quick joke. 'Yes, it's also 2003' is funny because Chandler cites an irrelevant detail (the year) with complete confidence as evidence. The structure is sharp and the delivery would sell it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God! I missed it! I missed the window!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? What window? We can get another window.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, Chandler, my ovulation window! It's gone!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And I just realized... I also forgot to pay the electric bill and it's due TODAY!

jokes.text: I may be done ovulating! I may have also served some very questionable meat at the restaurant.
jokes.setup: Monica panics that she may have missed her ovulation window.
jokes.punchline: In her flustered state, Monica also confesses she may have served bad meat at her restaurant — a completely separate professional crisis that surfaces in the same panicked breath.
jokes.explanation: Funny escalation joke — Monica's panic spirals to include a second, unrelated catastrophe. The non-sequitur reveal about the meat is funny but not developed enough to fully land. Good character integration (Monica as a chef makes this specific).

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I was curious!

jokes.text: Hey, where are all my ovulation sticks? There's only one here. — I might have checked to see if I was ovulating a couple times. — Chandler. — I am not working! There's not much to do around here!
jokes.setup: Monica discovers most of her ovulation test sticks are missing.
jokes.punchline: Chandler admits he was using them out of boredom — establishing that he's so unstimulated staying home that he's been repeatedly testing himself for ovulation. His defensive 'I am not working!' adds pathos.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. The image of Chandler repeatedly taking ovulation tests out of boredom is very specific, very strange, and very funny. His justification ('I am not working!') turns it into a portrait of stay-at-home despair. High character integration — this joke is specifically about Chandler's season-long jobless storyline.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I guess I'm buying him a drink.

jokes.text: Is there a woman waiting at the bar? Someone average height, dark hair? Or perhaps doing a puzzle?
jokes.setup: Ross arrives at the restaurant to meet his blind date.
jokes.punchline: He asks if someone is at the bar — then adds 'or perhaps doing a puzzle,' revealing that he's been told enough about her to know her hobbies and is half-hoping, half-dreading he'll find exactly that.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the puzzle detail from earlier. 'Or perhaps doing a puzzle' is a small, well-placed laugh that connects Ross's scene to the scheming subplot. Character-consistent with Ross's earnestness.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to have another drink. Because let's face it, by the end of the night I'm either going to be drunk or depressed, and drunk is more fun.

jokes.text: Uh, there's a drunk Chinese guy.
jokes.setup: Ross asks the waiter if a woman matching his date's description is waiting.
jokes.punchline: The waiter's completely flat response — 'there's a drunk Chinese guy' — is both useless and oddly specific. The deadpan delivery of irrelevant information is the whole joke.
jokes.explanation: Very economical joke — five words do the entire job. The specificity ('drunk Chinese guy') versus the vagueness Ross asked about (average height, dark hair) is a funny mismatch. Sets up the running gag about the Chinese guy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She didn't show up. I waited for two hours.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: At least she didn't show up with someone else.

jokes.text: Well, if I'm still here in an hour, buy him a drink on me.
jokes.setup: The waiter tells Ross there's a drunk Chinese guy at the bar instead of his date.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately resigns himself to being stood up and plans his miserable evening — buying a drink for his only bar companion, the drunk stranger.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke. The resigned humor of planning to drink with a stranger rather than a date is very Ross — he immediately begins catastrophizing while trying to maintain dignity.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm still ovulating.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And I'm still not ready.

jokes.text: I don't know if I should. I don't wanna be drunk when I...go home alone tonight.
jokes.setup: The waiter offers Ross more wine as he waits alone at the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Ross trails off mid-sentence, then completes it with self-pity — 'go home alone tonight.' The pause before the sad truth lands as both funny and weirdly touching.
jokes.explanation: Solid self-pity joke. The pause-and-complete structure lets the audience fill in the blank before Ross does, making the punchline land with mild anticipation. Ross's self-awareness about his sad situation is well-played.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't perform.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more dramatic?

jokes.text: Are you worried your date came, saw you and left?
jokes.setup: Ross says getting stood up is 'no big deal.'
jokes.punchline: The waiter cuts to the most brutal possible interpretation — that she DID come, looked at Ross, and left. It's a cruelty delivered with professional pleasantness.
jokes.explanation: Funny because the waiter's question is exactly what Ross is afraid of but would never say out loud. It's the dark subtext made text. The 'NO!' reaction (implied by the timestamp gap) is also a beat. Sets up the callback at [20:38].

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Did you just say 'making the beast with two backs'? What are we, pirates?

jokes.text: No! [long pause — reaction beat as Ross clearly begins to doubt himself]
jokes.setup: Waiter asks if Ross worries his date came, saw him, and left
jokes.punchline: Ross's emphatic 'No!' followed by visible self-doubt — the audience can see him convincing himself — is the visual punchline
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom reaction beat. The 'No!' that is immediately clearly a 'maybe' reads from David Schwimmer's facial performance. The timestamp gap (09:54 to 09:59) confirms a beat of silence following the denial. Strong visual comedy inferred from context.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: B-I-T-C-H!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A-S-S!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That spells baby!

jokes.text: Oh, good, because as of 4:00 this afternoon, I am not. — So let's do this. — I don't think I can. — Oh, come on. I know you're not 18 anymore, but give it a minute.
jokes.setup: Monica confirms she's still ovulating; the pressure is now on Chandler to perform.
jokes.punchline: Chandler hesitates; Monica's response — 'I know you're not 18 anymore, but give it a minute' — is both encouraging and subtly insulting about his age and stamina.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy about the pressure-driven sex of fertility planning. Monica's 'not 18 anymore' is a mild barb with an encouraging spin. Decent but not particularly fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You remember that bed-and-breakfast where the deer came through the window?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I was not responsible for that! That deer just... appeared!

jokes.text: 'Canoodling'? — Well, I can't say 'hump' or 'screw' in front of the B-A-B-Y.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are debating having sex with Emma in the room, and Monica uses the word 'canoodling.'
jokes.punchline: Monica spells out 'hump' and 'screw' to protect the baby — but the act of spelling out words the baby can't understand anyway, while standing next to her, is absurd. Also, 'canoodling' is itself a funny word for the act.
jokes.explanation: Decent joke about parental euphemism anxiety. Spelling out 'hump' and 'screw' to a baby who obviously can't understand is a funny absurdity. 'Canoodling' as the alternative is a funny word choice.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You look really good today.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: Oh, thanks. Yeah, well, I'm thinking of getting some work done. You know, just a little nip and tuck here and there.

jokes.text: I guess having sex in front of a baby isn't so... — Horrifying? Scarring? Something people go to jail for?
jokes.setup: Chandler trails off trying to rationalize having sex in front of Emma.
jokes.punchline: Monica completes his sentence with three escalating options — horrifying, scarring, then 'something people go to jail for' — each landing harder than the last.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke. The structure of Monica providing increasingly severe completions to Chandler's trailing sentence works well, and 'something people go to jail for' is the perfect final escalation. The rhythm of the three options (adjective, adjective, full clause) gives it comedic momentum.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You must be really rich to be with me.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I'm not that rich.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, you must be really good looking then.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm... I'm not that good looking either.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So what is it then?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I have no idea.

jokes.text: At that bed-and-breakfast, we didn't have sex because you thought a deer was staring through the window. — Well, what kind of a sick bastard wants to do it in front of a deer?
jokes.setup: Monica challenges Chandler's inhibition about having sex in front of Emma, citing a previous incident.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's moral indignation about the deer — 'what kind of sick bastard wants to do it in front of a deer?' — is delivered as a principled stance, as if the deer's feelings are the real concern.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The logic is completely inverted — Chandler is the one with an exhibitionism 'concern,' but he frames it as moral outrage on behalf of the deer. 'What kind of sick bastard' applied to himself-but-about-a-deer is unexpected, specific, and highly quotable. The specificity of a deer at a bed-and-breakfast is a perfect absurdist detail. Originality and structure both earn high scores.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: I'm not funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, at least you're self-aware.

jokes.text: Wow, everything looks so good. I think I'm gonna have the chicken.
jokes.setup: Rachel is on her terrible blind date with Steve, who hasn't yet revealed how awful he is.
jokes.punchline: The camera presumably shows Steve — this mundane statement about food is the last moment of normalcy before Steve starts destroying the date. The juxtaposition with what follows makes it retroactively funny.
jokes.explanation: More of a structural beat than a joke — it sets up the cringe sequence. Weak on its own but functional as a transition into the Steve comedy. Below average score reflects that it's doing setup work rather than landing a laugh.

jokes.text: You're really beautiful. — Oh. Wow, that's very sweet. — [CHUCKLES] I'm kind of funny-looking.
jokes.setup: Steve compliments Rachel, and she thanks him — a normal date exchange.
jokes.punchline: Steve immediately undermines himself: 'I'm kind of funny-looking.' The pivot from compliment to self-deprecation happens so fast it barely allows Rachel to respond.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe opener for the Steve sequence. The compliment-to-self-deprecation whiplash establishes Steve as a walking disaster immediately. The chuckle before the self-criticism makes it feel like he's sharing a known truth he finds mildly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Come on, there has to be something positive about owning a restaurant.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: Well, I guess the good news is I don't own it anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: I lost it to my addiction.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Gambling?

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: Cooking.

jokes.text: Look, I mean, come on...you're way out of my league. Everybody in here knows it. I bet that guy over there is probably saying: 'Ooh, why's she out with him? He must be rich.' Well, I'm not.
jokes.setup: Steve has established he thinks he's funny-looking. Now he escalates to full self-destruction.
jokes.punchline: He constructs a hypothetical compliment ('he must be rich') and then immediately refutes it ('Well, I'm not') — actively disproving every possible redeeming quality in advance.
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe escalation. Steve's pre-emptive destruction of every possible attractive quality is a good comedic device. The rhythm of constructing and immediately dismantling the hypothetical compliment is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So what do you do?

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: I work at Bloomingdale's.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, that's nice. What do you do there?

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: I'm in charge of the men's department. I fold shirts.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You fold shirts?

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: Yeah, all day long. Fold, fold, fold. It's a dream come true.

jokes.text: I'm not funny, either. So if you were thinking, 'Well, he's not that good-looking, but maybe we'll have some laughs,' that ain't gonna happen.
jokes.setup: Steve has established he's not rich, not good-looking.
jokes.punchline: He now preemptively eliminates 'funny' — again constructing the audience's last hope and immediately dashing it. The list of negative qualities is building to absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Good continuation of Steve's self-destruction sequence. The pattern is becoming clear (he eliminates every possible redeeming quality), and 'that ain't gonna happen' has a nice finality to it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not a catch. I'm not even a good throw-in.

jokes.text: Well, come on, Steve, let's not rule out nervous laughter. Ha-ha-ha.
jokes.setup: Steve says there won't be any laughs on this date.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's desperate offer of 'nervous laughter' as a consolation prize — punctuated by her demonstrating it immediately — is both a good save and an admission that she's already nervous and uncomfortable.
jokes.explanation: Rachel's response is well-crafted — it's simultaneously empathetic, in-denial, and self-aware. The 'ha-ha-ha' demonstration makes it land harder. Good character work showing Rachel trying to maintain social grace in an impossible situation.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What do you like about yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: Well, I guess my hair.

jokes.text: Hey, now, wait a minute, Phoebe told me that you owned your own restaurant. That's impressive. — I lost it to drugs.
jokes.setup: Rachel tries to find something positive about Steve — he owned a restaurant.
jokes.punchline: He lost it to drugs. Full stop. No elaboration. The brevity and finality are what make it devastating and funny.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and the best single line in the Steve sequence. The structure is perfect: Rachel builds up an impressive credential ('owned your own restaurant'), Steve confirms it, then destroys it in three words. 'I lost it to drugs' has near-perfect economy — there's no better version of this joke in more words. The pause before the reveal (inferred from the timestamp gap at 12:37) adds to the impact. This approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Steve, you can't be serious. Have you looked in a mirror? Your hair looks like a dead animal that got into a fight with a blender.

jokes.text: I silk-screen T-shirts now. — Really? What's that like? — It's really fulfilling doing something you hate for no money.
jokes.setup: After losing his restaurant to drugs, Steve describes his current work.
jokes.punchline: 'It's really fulfilling doing something you hate for no money' — the sarcasm is thick, delivered straight, and is a genuinely good line about the misery of the gig economy / underemployment.
jokes.explanation: A legitimately great line. 'Really fulfilling doing something you hate for no money' is quotable outside the episode's context — it captures universal work misery. The construction is excellent: the setup ('really fulfilling') signals sarcasm, but the specific double negative of 'hate' + 'no money' sells it. High quotability justified.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that guy you set me up with was a nightmare.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? He seemed nice!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Nice? He spent the whole dinner talking about his ex-girlfriend's bunions!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm so sorry!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? If you ever set me up with anyone again, I will kill you. I will actually murder you.

jokes.text: That's right. I have no money, I'm not funny, I live in a studio apartment with two other guys. And I'm pretty sure I'm infertile.
jokes.setup: Steve continues cataloguing his failures.
jokes.punchline: The escalation reaches its peak with 'I'm pretty sure I'm infertile' — which is not only the most intimate detail but also medical, suggesting a whole additional layer of personal tragedy being disclosed to a stranger on a first date.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke. 'I'm pretty sure I'm infertile' is the perfect final item in the list because it's the most personal, the most medically specific, and comes with 'pretty sure' — which implies he doesn't even have confirmed bad news, just a suspicion he's sharing with a first date. The 'pretty sure' qualifier is excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't believe you set me up with Steve. He was a nightmare!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, he's not that bad. He's just... misunderstood. And maybe a little socially awkward. Okay, fine, he's terrible, but I didn't know that when I set you up!

jokes.text: Now, come on. Come on, Steve. There must be something that you like about yourself. — I do like my hair.
jokes.setup: Rachel desperately tries to find one positive thing Steve likes about himself after the full catalogue of disasters.
jokes.punchline: After all the profound failures (drugs, poverty, infertility), Steve's one positive is... he likes his hair. The bathos of the response is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Excellent bathos. After infertility, drug addiction, and poverty, 'I do like my hair' is the most trivially shallow silver lining possible. The gap between the depth of his problems and the pettiness of his self-affirmation is the whole joke. Followed presumably by Rachel's reaction beat (really? with that hair?) — the [13:18] silence/reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, he's going through a lot right now. His mother never hugged him, and his father was very critical, and he has this thing where he can't process emotions properly, so he acts out.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, he's using drugs right now.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Well, that explains it.

jokes.text: Phoebe, it's me! I'm going to hunt you down and kill you.
jokes.setup: Rachel calls Phoebe during the worst date of her life.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's immediate threat — 'hunt you down and kill you' — is delivered as a completely reasonable response rather than an overreaction, which is what makes it funny. It's the most extreme version of 'this date is bad.'
jokes.explanation: Good delivery-dependent joke. The humor is entirely in the calm certainty of a death threat as a date review. Functional but not especially original — 'I'll kill you for this' as a complaint about a bad setup is fairly standard.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Are we running from the law or are we going to Mexico for spring break? Because I have two completely different outfits planned.

jokes.text: You know, you are talking about one of my dear, dear friends. — I don't care. This guy is a nightmare. — All right, so he gets a little crazy when he's stoned. — He's not stoned. — Did he go out for a cigarette? — Yeah. Four times. — My dear, sweet Rach.
jokes.setup: Rachel complains that Steve is a nightmare; Phoebe defends him.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's response to 'he's not stoned' is to ask if he went out for a cigarette — which he did, four times — and her 'my dear, sweet Rach' is a knowing, resigned acknowledgment that yes, he is very stoned and terrible.
jokes.explanation: Good multi-beat joke. The reveal that Steve has been 'going out for cigarettes' four times explains his erratic behavior and also adds to his portrait as a disaster. 'My dear, sweet Rach' as Phoebe's benediction is very Phoebe — a phrase of affectionate helplessness. Character integration for Phoebe is high.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why are you playing peekaboo by yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not by myself. Ben's here. He started it.

jokes.text: Well, our plan is working. Rachel's having a miserable time...and Ross is just stood up somewhere at a restaurant all alone. Great. Pretty soon they'll be back together. By the time anyone's figured out what we've done, we'll be in sunny Mexico.
jokes.setup: Phoebe reports to Joey that the plan is working.
jokes.punchline: 'By the time anyone figures out what we've done, we'll be in sunny Mexico' — Phoebe has apparently added a getaway plan to their romantic intervention, as if setting up a bad date is a crime requiring international flight.
jokes.explanation: Good Phoebe absurdism. The escalation from 'sweet matchmaking plan' to 'we need to flee to Mexico' is a funny logical leap that only Phoebe would take. It treats a minor social manipulation as a heist that requires an escape route.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You can't just say certain words around children. You have to spell them out.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Like, 'Don't be a B-I-T-C-H' or 'Stop being such a D-I-C-K.'

jokes.text: Oh, wait, that's the end of a different plan.
jokes.setup: Phoebe mentions fleeing to Mexico.
jokes.punchline: She clarifies that the Mexico escape is actually from a DIFFERENT plan — implying she has multiple active plans with their own getaway strategies. This adds a whole alarming dimension to Phoebe's inner life.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and the highest-scoring Phoebe moment. The notion that Phoebe has a DIFFERENT, SEPARATE plan that also ends in fleeing to Mexico is delightfully bizarre and character-perfect. It suggests a rich inner life of schemes, each with their own international escape routes. High character integration: this joke could ONLY be Phoebe. The delivery is perfectly economy — one sentence does enormous world-building work. Comparable in character specificity and surprise to the 8.0 benchmark anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know, I've been stood up before, but at least those women had the decency to call. I mean, what kind of person just doesn't show up? And then you're left here, alone, eating free crab cakes, which is great, don't get me wrong, but it really makes you think about what you're doing wrong. I mean, is it something I said? Is it the way I dress? Because I can change. I'm very adaptable. And sexually, I'm very... I'm very open-minded. I mean, there are things I'm willing to try that most guys wouldn't even—

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Sir, I'm just here to refill your water.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Right, right, of course. But if you know anyone...

jokes.text: What are you doing? — Emma was doing it.
jokes.setup: Monica enters to find Chandler doing something (presumably crawling or making baby sounds to entertain Emma).
jokes.punchline: 'Emma was doing it' — Chandler has been copying the baby's behavior, and his defense is that he was following her lead.
jokes.explanation: Quick physical comedy beat. The specific visual of Chandler mimicking a baby's behavior and defending it with 'Emma was doing it' is funny for how committed it implies he was to the baby's activity. Visual gag dependent on what exactly he was doing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So what's this about a waiters' pool?

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Oh, we're betting on how long your marriage lasts.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've got fifty bucks on six months.

jokes.text: And you can't make any noise. — Okay, I'll try.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are trying to have sex quietly while Emma is asleep.
jokes.punchline: 'Okay, I'll try' — Chandler's response to 'you can't make any noise' implies he's not confident he can be quiet, which is itself a small admission.
jokes.explanation: Functional but weak joke. 'I'll try' as a response to noise restriction is a mild implication, but it's not developed enough. The earlier 'I'll try to stop' joke (#26) is a better use of the same construction.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Look, it was fast, okay? I barely got my pants off.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Fast? Chandler, you weren't even in the room yet when it was over.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I was nervous!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You were in the hallway!

jokes.text: Why is the bedroom door closed? [CHANDLER & MONICA MOANING]
jokes.setup: Joey finds Emma alone and wonders where the babysitters are.
jokes.punchline: Joey asks aloud why the bedroom door is closed — and the answer immediately arrives: moaning from inside. The question-answer timing is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic door-moan comedy timing. The question 'why is the bedroom door closed?' followed immediately by the answer (moaning) is a well-executed sitcom beat. High economy because the structure carries all the humor.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: If you guys lost her, I'm gonna kill you. I'm gonna kill you and then I'm gonna steal a baby.

jokes.text: You can't have S-E-X when you're taking care of a B-A-B-I-E.
jokes.setup: Joey discovers Chandler and Monica are having sex while babysitting Emma.
jokes.punchline: Joey spells out both 'sex' and 'baby' — but misspells 'baby' as 'B-A-B-I-E' — directly echoing Monica's earlier spelling convention while revealing Joey doesn't know how to spell 'baby.'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke, and one of the best in the season. This works on three layers simultaneously: (1) it callbacks perfectly to Monica's spelling convention, showing Joey learned from her; (2) it's a principled moral stance from Joey, which is funny because he's not usually principled; (3) the misspelling of 'baby' as 'B-A-B-I-E' reveals Joey absorbed the FORM of the joke without the content — he picked up the spelling habit but can't spell the word. All three layers pay off at once, in one sentence. This is comparable to the Snip-snap anchor in terms of character integration and surprise. Highly quotable and absolutely earns rewatch bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's okay to cry. There's no shame in it.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: I'm not crying!

jokes.text: I've got bad news. The Chinese guy left.
jokes.setup: Ross has been waiting alone at the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: The waiter treats the Chinese man's departure as 'bad news' for Ross — confirming that the drunk stranger was Ross's only companion for the evening, and his loss is a genuine social setback.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to the Chinese man from earlier. The waiter delivering this as 'bad news' treats the drunk stranger as Ross's de facto companion — a very funny social commentary on how low Ross's evening has sunk. Economy is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Look, I didn't kidnap her, okay? I was doing performance art. You know, like Yoko Ono.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not performance art, that's kidnapping.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, maybe Yoko started the same way!

jokes.text: Eh, if it was meant to be, it's meant to be.
jokes.setup: The waiter tells Ross the Chinese guy left, implying this is a loss.
jokes.punchline: Ross responds with a romantic-destiny platitude — typically applied to love — but here applied to his fleeting relationship with a drunk stranger. The grandiosity of 'meant to be' in this context is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke. Using a romantic-destiny phrase for a drunk bar stranger is a funny application of the wrong emotional framework. Ross's resignation (and slight romanticism about everything) is very character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So you guys... you know, did the deed?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How'd you know? His hair!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Look at his hair! He's been very sexual!

jokes.text: Wow, free crab cakes? Well, that's nice. Although I was hoping to have sex tonight.
jokes.setup: A waiter offers Ross free crab cake appetizers as consolation for being stood up.
jokes.punchline: Ross accepts the consolation prize with apparent gratitude, then adds that he had been hoping for sex — the two things presented as equivalent in his current emotional state.
jokes.explanation: Very good joke. The bathos of treating 'free crab cakes' and 'sex' as roughly comparable consolation prizes is perfectly executed. Ross's matter-of-fact confession to a stranger waiter ('I was hoping to have sex tonight') is both over-sharing and disarmingly honest.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do you know how much those things cost?

jokes.text: Uh, okay, um, the waiters have a little pool going. We have a bet on how long it'll take before you give up and go home.
jokes.setup: Ross has been pitied with free crab cakes; another waiter rushes in to stop it.
jokes.punchline: The waiter reveals the staff has an actual betting pool on Ross's misery — the hospitality profession's dark underbelly exposed. The pool on 'when he gives up and goes home' is bleakly specific.
jokes.explanation: Good dark joke. The waiters betting on how long it takes Ross to give up is a funny institutional cruelty — the restaurant as a machine that profits from romantic failure. The reveal makes the free crab cakes retroactively sinister.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm gonna tell Rachel you ate her cheesecake.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What do you want?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I want naming rights. When I have a kid, I get to name him.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No way.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Then Rachel finds out about the cheesecake.

jokes.text: What? You're making money off my misery? — Well, if you stay till 9:20, I am.
jokes.setup: Ross is outraged that the waiters have a pool on his misery.
jokes.punchline: The waiter's response is entirely mercenary — confirming the bet and specifying the exact time Ross needs to stay to make the waiter money. Total honesty in a moment demanding sympathy.
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy joke. The waiter doesn't deny the cruelty — he just helpfully specifies the profit condition. '9:20' as the specific time makes it funnier than a vague answer would. The mercenary specificity is what elevates this.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I want to have kids so I can pass on the Tribbiani name.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you're not even passing on your genes.

jokes.text: I have never been so insulted in my life. Now, if you'll wrap up my free crab cakes, I'll be on my way.
jokes.setup: Ross delivers an indignant speech about never being so insulted.
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks for the free crab cakes to be wrapped up — taking the consolation prize from his humiliators before he storms out. The indignation and the crab cake request coexist perfectly.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Ross moments. The juxtaposition of righteous indignation with immediately requesting the free food is a perfect character joke — Ross is wounded but also practical. The formal request ('if you'll wrap up my free crab cakes') while in full 'insulted dignity' mode is very Ross. High quotability — the line structure is memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I admit it. My plan didn't work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But in my defense, it was a really good plan. It just... had one tiny flaw.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Actually, it had like... a lot of flaws. But who's counting?

jokes.text: Well, that was weird. You were loud and I was fast.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica emerge from the bedroom having hurriedly had sex while Emma was asleep.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's post-coital assessment — 'you were loud and I was fast' — is a clinical debrief of a disaster, with Chandler admitting his speed as a failure rather than a success.
jokes.explanation: Very good joke. 'You were loud and I was fast' is a perfect six-word post-mortem of terrible sex. Chandler's willingness to immediately identify and own his failure (speed) while also noting Monica's (volume) is both funny and character-consistent — he processes everything through self-deprecating honesty. High economy.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: So what do you say? Want to get coffee sometime?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Oh, I wish I didn't have to wait to take a pregnancy test. — [CHUCKLES] You may wanna get some more of those too.
jokes.setup: Monica hopes their rushed sex worked and wishes she could immediately test.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'you may wanna get some more of those too' — a callback to his having used up all the ovulation tests — now implies he might also burn through pregnancy tests with the same boredom-driven curiosity.
jokes.explanation: Good callback. Chandler's suggestion to stock up on pregnancy tests implies he'll use those for entertainment too. The callback adds value and extends the character joke without being too on-the-nose about it.

dialogue.line:
Being rejected for sex

Admitting impotence as final self-sabotage

jokes.text: Oh, my God, where's Emma? Where's Emma? — Don't ask me. I was in there canoodling you.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler realize Emma is missing.
jokes.punchline: Chandler uses 'canoodling' — Monica's earlier euphemism — in his defense of not knowing where Emma is. The callback to their earlier spelling/euphemism conversation adds a layer.
jokes.explanation: Good callback joke. Chandler adopting Monica's 'canoodling' euphemism for the defense is funny because he's the one who questioned the word in the first place. The callback is tight but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What do you think?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Um, where did you get this?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Do you like it?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's... it's very... What size is it?

jokes.text: You better hope we're pregnant...because one way or another, we're giving a baby back to Rachel!
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler panic about Emma being missing.
jokes.punchline: Monica's threat that if they're pregnant they'll give THAT baby to Rachel is a dark escalation — she's so stressed she's contemplating giving away a hypothetical future child. The 'one way or another' adds to the gangster-threat energy.
jokes.explanation: Good dark joke. The logic is funny — Monica, in a panic, plans to give Rachel a baby either way. The 'one way or another' crime-thriller framing applied to baby logistics is a fun tonal mismatch.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God! I'm so sorry! I didn't know you guys were... I'll just go.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, it's okay. We were just—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, I get it. You guys are trying to make a baby. That's so sweet!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Actually, we're just... we like doing this.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Well, either way, you're gonna have so many kids. Let's see... I've walked in on you guys like, what, seven times this month? So if you keep this up, you're gonna have like... forty-seven babies by next year.

jokes.text: I can't believe I'm crying in front of you. You must think I'm so pathetic. — No, no, no, I admire a man who can cry. — Really? — Don't touch my coat!
jokes.setup: Steve has broken down crying in front of Rachel on their date. Rachel tries to be comforting.
jokes.punchline: Rachel says she admires men who can cry; Steve momentarily brightens ('Really?') and reaches for her coat — and Rachel's immediate 'Don't touch my coat!' reveals the comfort was entirely hollow and self-protective.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The misdirection is elegant: Rachel's 'I admire a man who can cry' sounds like genuine warmth, then 'Don't touch my coat!' instantly reveals it was a platitude with no accompanying intimacy. The specific pivot to the COAT — not a hug, not emotional closeness, but her protecting her coat — is a perfect character detail. Rachel's superficiality and self-preservation instinct captured in four words. High originality, structure, and character integration all justified.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! See? I told you guys my plan would work!

jokes.text: Oh, my God, this is the worst date ever. — [WHINES] Oh, come on. Look, you know what, I'm sorry, but did you really think that this was going well?
jokes.setup: Ross calls Rachel; she immediately tells him the date is terrible.
jokes.punchline: Ross's 'did you really think that this was going well?' — the question implies that from the outside, it was obviously a disaster, suggesting Rachel's level of self-delusion in staying through it.
jokes.explanation: Functional exchange — the irony of Ross criticizing Rachel's date when he was just stood up is appreciated but not particularly well-developed. Decent character interaction but below average for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Where should I run?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, um, well there's a really nice path behind the old hospital. But if you're wanted for murder, I'd suggest the subway tunnels.

jokes.text: Oh, thank God! Emma, there you are! — What? What do you mean, 'there you are'? Where was she? — Uh, we were playing peekaboo. She loves it when I'm dramatic. Heh.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica were panicking about Emma being missing; Chandler finds her and Rachel catches him.
jokes.punchline: Chandler improvises 'we were playing peekaboo, she loves it when I'm dramatic' — a transparently bad cover story delivered with maximum commitment. The 'heh' is perfect Chandler nervous energy.
jokes.explanation: Good Chandler improvisation joke. 'She loves it when I'm dramatic' is a funny specific detail for a made-up cover story. The lie is too elaborate to be believable but Chandler commits to it, which is very character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: My heart is like a baked potato... it used to be warm and satisfying, but now it's just cold and hard.

jokes.text: Why the hell did you take her? — Because you two were having sex! — No, we weren't. — Don't you lie to me. I can tell by Chandler's hair. You are so lazy. Can't you get on top for once?
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica deny having sex while babysitting.
jokes.punchline: Joey can tell they were having sex from Chandler's hair specifically — meaning he's read Chandler's post-sex hair before. His follow-up 'can't you get on top for once?' directed at Monica adds an unexpected layer of intimate knowledge and judgment.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Joey's ability to read Chandler's post-sex hair is a funny specific detail, but the kicker — 'can't you get on top for once?' — is what elevates it. Joey's intimate knowledge of their sex habits (derived from hair analysis, apparently) is both invasive and hilarious. It implies this has happened before. 'You are so lazy' to Monica is an unexpected character judgment from Joey that lands hard. High character integration for all three.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter 1
dialogue.line: I got twenty bucks says someone cries in the next five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter 2
dialogue.line: You're on.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.line: I just... I can't fit into my pants anymore. My thighs are huge. I used to be able to see my feet!

dialogue.speaker: Waiter 1
dialogue.line: Pay up.

jokes.text: Hey, I gotta. Unless... — Unless what? — Unless you name your first-born child Joey.
jokes.setup: Joey threatens to tell Rachel that Chandler and Monica were having sex while babysitting.
jokes.punchline: Joey's leverage demand is to name their first-born child Joey — a callback to his earlier 'someone has to carry on the family name' argument.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. Joey's ability to convert his eccentric wish into actual leverage is a funny plot development. The callback to the earlier 'family name' joke is well-structured, and Joey using emotional blackmail in service of a sincere naming goal is very Joey.

dialogue.line: Continuing breakdown: Escalating to most intimate self-hatred

jokes.text: Your family name is Tribbiani.
jokes.setup: Joey says someone needs to carry on 'my family name' by naming the baby Joey.
jokes.punchline: Chandler points out that naming the baby 'Joey' wouldn't actually perpetuate the family name — 'Joey' is a first name, and the family name is 'Tribbiani.' Joey's own plan is logically flawed.
jokes.explanation: Sharp logical takedown. Chandler correctly identifies the flaw in Joey's reasoning in five words, delivered with perfect deadpan. The beat that follows (Joey's pause before 'Oh ha ha') implies he almost fell for it before realizing Chandler was right. Very economical and character-specific for Chandler (the logical one).

jokes.text: Oh, ha, ha. You almost had me.
jokes.setup: Chandler points out that Joey's naming plan wouldn't actually perpetuate his family name.
jokes.punchline: Joey's 'you almost had me' implies he was briefly fooled by Chandler's logic (which was actually correct), and then recovered — but the recovery is wrong. Joey thinks Chandler was making a joke. He wasn't.
jokes.explanation: Excellent reaction beat. The genius of this joke is that Chandler was entirely correct, but Joey interprets the correct information as an attempted trick, laughs it off, and maintains his wrong position. This is a perfect Joey joke — his confidence in his own wrongness is impenetrable. Very high character integration: this response is specifically Joey and captures the character's signature inability to follow logic while believing he's the smart one.

jokes.text: Oh, ha, ha. You almost had me.
jokes.setup: Chandler has correctly pointed out that naming a child 'Joey' doesn't carry on the Tribbiani family name
jokes.punchline: Joey laughs it off — 'You almost had me' — as if Chandler were trying to trick him, rather than actually correcting him. Joey's confusion about who is outsmarting whom is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Joey's response treats Chandler's correct logical point as a clever trick, implying Joey still doesn't understand the flaw in his plan. 'You almost had me' is funny because Joey thinks he's the one who caught something, when in fact he's the one who was wrong. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Well, um... I think I know the answer to this question, but...would you like to make love to me? — Really, really not.
jokes.setup: The date has been catastrophic; Steve has cried, confessed drug addiction, infertility, and poverty.
jokes.punchline: Despite all of this, Steve asks if Rachel wants to 'make love' — with the qualifier 'I think I know the answer.' Rachel's response — 'really, really not' — is the most emphatically negative possible answer.
jokes.explanation: Very strong capper to the Steve date sequence. 'Would you like to make love to me?' as the conclusion to the worst date ever is perfect — the phrasing 'make love' adding a formal, romantic quality that makes the ask even more tone-deaf. The qualifier 'I think I know the answer' shows self-awareness but no self-control. 'Really, really not' is a great two-adverb rejection — the double 'really' escalating the certainty. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: It doesn't work anyway.
jokes.setup: Rachel has rejected Steve's advance. There's a pause.
jokes.punchline: Steve's 'it doesn't work anyway' — referring to his own sexual function — is both a final humiliation and a strangely admirable final honesty. The timing (after a pause) makes it land as an afterthought he felt compelled to add.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. The timing is everything — a beat after the rejection, as if he had to work up to saying it. 'It doesn't work anyway' as a coda to the entire Steve catastrophe is a perfect final detail. It adds to the 'I'm pretty sure I'm infertile' detail earlier, suggesting the problems are more than just infertility. Four words, enormous impact. Near-perfect economy. The understatement makes it devastating.

jokes.text: Hey, what's wrong? — I just had a rough night. — Oh. Crab cake?
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel bump into each other, both looking rough from their respective date disasters.
jokes.punchline: Ross's response to Rachel's distress is to offer her a crab cake — his wrapped-up restaurant consolation prize. The crab cake as the solution to emotional distress is a perfect callback payoff.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. Ross offering crab cakes as emotional support is funny on its own, but it's the physical proof that he actually took the crab cakes home that makes it special. The 'crab cake?' as a one-word offer of comfort is very economical. Rewatch bonus for the visual of Ross actually having the wrapped crab cakes.

jokes.text: Oh, no. Do you think she walked in, saw you and left? — Why does everyone keep saying that?
jokes.setup: Ross explains he got stood up at the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: 'Why does everyone keep saying that?' — the waiter's earlier brutal question (did she see you and leave?) has apparently been said to Ross multiple times. The callback lands harder because it implies the cruelty was repeated by multiple people.
jokes.explanation: Very good callback. 'Why does everyone keep saying that?' is a perfect payoff — the audience knows it was the waiter, but 'everyone' implies the humiliation has become a chorus. Ross's wounded bewilderment is completely in character. This is how callbacks should work — the second hit is funnier than the first.

jokes.text: If it makes you feel any better, I wish my date hadn't shown up. — That bad? — Well, he makes T-shirts for a living...and he thought it would be appropriate to give me...this. 'Female Body Inspector'? — What size is that?
jokes.setup: Rachel tells Ross her date was awful and shows him the T-shirt she was given.
jokes.punchline: Ross's response to seeing the 'Female Body Inspector' T-shirt isn't sympathy or outrage — it's 'What size is that?' The implication being he might actually want it.
jokes.explanation: Good laugh. Rachel expects commiseration but gets Ross checking the shirt size. 'Female Body Inspector' as Steve's silk-screen product is a perfect callback to his job, and Ross's interest in the shirt is a surprising and character-consistent male response. The joke recontextualizes Ross and Rachel's relationship beat with a funny undercutting.

jokes.text: Now wait a minute. — So they'll name their first child Joey? — Uh-huh. — How do I get them to name the next one after me? — It's easy. You just walk in on them having sex. — Oh, so they owe me, like, three Phoebes.
jokes.setup: Joey tells Phoebe about the naming deal he extracted from Chandler and Monica.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately strategizes to get the same deal — and realizes she's already walked in on them enough times to be owed three Phoebes. The implication that Phoebe has a history of walking in on them is funny and vaguely alarming.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and an excellent escalation of the naming gag. 'Three Phoebes' as a quantity is a perfect absurdist unit of measurement, and the implication that Phoebe has walked in on Chandler and Monica at least three times is both alarming and completely plausible given her character. High character integration — the joke works because Phoebe's combination of strategic thinking and accidental voyeurism is very specific. 'Three Phoebes' is immediately quotable.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Look, it's Ross and Rachel! The plan is working! [LAUGHS MANIACALLY] — Don't do the plan laugh.
jokes.setup: Phoebe sees Ross and Rachel bonding and launches into the plan laugh.
jokes.punchline: Joey shuts her down — 'Don't do the plan laugh' — a reversal of roles (Joey was the one who was shushed before) and an acknowledgment that the laugh is officially dead.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. Phoebe launching the plan laugh one more time and Joey stopping her is a satisfying closing of the running gag. The role reversal (Joey now being the responsible one) adds a small extra layer.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Look, it's Ross and Rachel! The plan is working! [LAUGHS MANIACALLY]
jokes.setup: Phoebe spots Ross and Rachel talking together from across the coffee house
jokes.punchline: She immediately deploys the plan laugh one more time
jokes.explanation: The final deployment of the plan laugh running gag. It works as a callback but doesn't add new comedic dimension — it's purely a callback payoff. Functional but diminishing returns compared to earlier iterations.

jokes.text: The first dates we've had in months, and they were both such disasters. — Oh. Huh. You know, it is weird that Phoebe would set me up on a date that was awful...on the same night Joey set you up on a date that didn't even show.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel commiserate about their terrible dating nights.
jokes.punchline: Ross starts to put the pieces together — the double disaster is too convenient. The audience is ahead of him, waiting for the penny to drop.
jokes.explanation: Functional plot beat more than a joke. The 'putting it together' moment is necessary for the story but doesn't deliver a strong laugh on its own. Competent but below the episode average.

jokes.text: Wait a minute. — You don't think it was intentional? — I mean, that's just stupid. — We're geniuses. Huh? — Look at them! They're really bonding. — They're falling in love all over again.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel suspect something is off. Across the coffee shop, Joey and Phoebe watch and celebrate.
jokes.punchline: While Ross and Rachel dismiss the scheming as 'just stupid,' Joey and Phoebe celebrate being 'geniuses' — the dramatic irony of two smart people not suspecting two not-smart people is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke built on dramatic irony. 'That's just stupid' / 'We're geniuses' in immediate juxtaposition is the kind of sitcom intercutting that works well on film. The irony that Joey and Phoebe's plan is both stupid and effective is a nice thematic touch.

jokes.text: Oh, they see us. Oh, they look mad. — Oh, they figured it out. They're coming. Run! — Where? — Mexico!
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel have figured out the scheme. Joey and Phoebe start to panic.
jokes.punchline: 'Run! Where? Mexico!' — Phoebe's earlier Mexico plan is now activated. The callback lands perfectly as the episode's closing escalation. Joey's 'Where?' shows he had no escape plan at all.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and an excellent closing callback. The Mexico plan from 20 minutes earlier pays off perfectly — Phoebe had an escape plan, and when crisis hits, she deploys it. Joey's 'Where?' is the perfect beat (he was never told the escape plan), and 'Mexico!' is the most satisfying possible answer. The structure builds from panic, to question, to absurd answer in three words. Economy is excellent. This is how you close a running gag — the Mexico callback lands bigger than any of the intermediate plan-laugh bits.

jokes.text: Can you believe they're still not here? I know. A double blind date and we both get stood up. What are the chances?
jokes.setup: Two new people at the restaurant complain that their blind dates haven't shown up.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that there's another couple who were also stood up — but this is not played as a coincidence, it's the implicit echo of Ross's situation from a different angle. The final tag suggests a world full of blind-date disasters.
jokes.explanation: Functional tag scene setup. These are new characters with no established comedy, so the joke isn't particularly funny on its own — it's structural, setting up the final gag.

jokes.text: Could we have our free crab cakes now? — What? — We've been stood up. And we want our free crab cakes. — Guys, give it a rest. Nobody's betting on you tonight. Although we do have a pool going to see how long it takes that guy to cry.
jokes.setup: Two people ask for free crab cakes because they've been stood up — clearly they heard about Ross's arrangement.
jokes.punchline: The waiter denies them crab cakes ('nobody's betting on you') but reveals there IS a pool — on a crying man at the bar. The crying pool reveals the restaurant has a whole ongoing system of profiting from patron misery.
jokes.explanation: Good closing joke with multiple callback layers. The crab cake callback works; the pool-on-crying callback is an excellent expansion of the waiter-betting-on-misery concept. The implication that the crying man at the bar is Steve (crying from the date) adds a final connection between the two storylines.

jokes.text: Could we have our free crab cakes now? — What? — We've been stood up. And we want our free crab cakes. — Guys, give it a rest. Nobody's betting on you tonight.
jokes.setup: The stood-up couple asks for free crab cakes, using Ross's example as precedent
jokes.punchline: The waiter denies them — there's no bet running on them, so there's no interest in keeping them there — confirming the crab cakes were entirely transactional
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the crab cakes and the bet return to close the restaurant subplot. The revelation that the crab cakes were only offered to keep Ross there longer (for the bet) is confirmed by their denial to this couple. Economical and structurally satisfying.

jokes.text: I have such fat hands!
jokes.setup: The waiter mentions there's a pool on how long it takes a man at the bar to cry.
jokes.punchline: Steve's voice: 'I have such fat hands!' — a sudden, random outcry about his hands being fat. After everything we've heard about Steve (drugs, poverty, infertility, can't perform, bad hair), fat hands is both absurd and entirely consistent with his self-pity spiral.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best closing joke and a competitor for the best single joke of the episode alongside the B-A-B-I-E spelling. After an episode of Steve cataloguing massive failures (drug addiction, lost restaurant, poverty, infertility, sexual dysfunction), the final item in his self-loathing list is 'I have such fat hands!' The bathos is perfect — the gap between the profound tragedies and this petty complaint is enormous. It's also a callback to Steve's one moment of self-affirmation ('I do like my hair'), suggesting his positive self-view has collapsed entirely. 'Fat hands' as the final indignity is a perfect absurdist capstone. Economy: four words, biggest laugh. High character integration because only Steve could cry about fat hands after everything else. Earns its high scores.

tmdb_overview: Phoebe and Joey purposely set Ross and Rachel up on bad dates in the hopes they'll get back together. Meanwhile, Monica and Chandler babysit Emma, and aren't being as responsible as they should be.
insight: Blind date premise fuels 70 jokes in 42 minutes—character friction hits peak cringe.
